chapter_title: Interacting with Smart Contract Data (Read-Only Operations)

screens.title: Interacting with Smart Contract Data (Read-Only)
screens.subtitle: Create contract instances, call view/pure functions, and read public state without gas

narration.text: In this chapter we learn how a frontend reads data from deployed smart contracts without creating transactions. You will see how an application's provider, the contract address, and the contract ABI work together so your JavaScript code can ask a node for data. I will show concrete patterns in both Web3. js and Ethers. js, explain why getters for public variables are generated automatically by the compiler, and make the crucial distinction between calling read-only functions and sending state-changing transactions. Practically, you will learn to instantiate a contract with its address and ABI, call view and pure functions to fetch values, and wrap calls in error handling so your DApp fails gracefully when a node is unavailable or the ABI is out of date. As a concrete example, we will use a SimpleData contract that exposes a message and a counter, and call getMessageLength and multiplyByTwo to see immediate, gas-free results. A key misconception we will correct early is to never expect state changes from using call(); it only reads. By the end you will understand the minimal pieces required to show contract state in a UI and how to avoid common pitfalls when wiring ABI and address into your code.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Read-only contract interactions use only a provider plus the contract's ABI and address. They return data locally and do not cost gas or require signing.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to instantiate contract objects, call read-only functions, and safely display on-chain data in a frontend. First, you will learn to create a contract instance in both Web3. js and Ethers. js using the contract's deployed address and the ABI generated by your compiler. Second, you will make view and pure calls that retrieve data from the node without submitting a transaction. Third, you will read compiler-generated public variable getters and convert results into UI-friendly formats. Finally, you will implement robust error handling: wrap asynchronous calls in try catch blocks, surface friendly messages for network or ABI mismatches, and avoid the common mistake of expecting state changes from call operations. Each objective pairs a clear action with why it matters, for example: calling a view function to show a live counter in your DApp without spending gas. These skills let your application stay responsive while respecting blockchain costs and user expectations.

keyIdea.title: Objectives summary
keyIdea.text: Learn to instantiate contracts, call view/pure functions, read public variables, and handle read-only errors in your DApp.

narration.text: This second objectives slide emphasizes practical application and reliability. You will practice calling functions with both Web3. js and Ethers. js, converting numeric results to strings when necessary, and using the provider-only instantiation pattern to avoid unintended transactions. You will also verify ABI correctness by testing simple getter calls and learn to interpret common error messages like function not found or invalid arguments. Apply and verify

This slide focuses on hands-on checks and diagnostics you should perform when reading data from a contract.

  • Instantiation check: Confirm ABI and address match the deployed contract before calling functions.
  • Provider-only reads: Use provider to avoid signing requirements and keep calls gas-free.
  • Data conversion: Convert BigNumber results to strings for UI display or number formats.
  • Error handling: Wrap calls in try catch and present clear user messages on failure.
Quick checklist
Compile and copy ABI, deploy and copy address, paste both into your read script, run and verify outputs. If you see function not found, update the ABI.

screens.title: Contract Instance: Address + ABI
screens.subtitle: Why these two pieces let your frontend speak to a deployed contract

narration.text: A contract instance is the local JavaScript representation of a deployed smart contract. To build one you need two immutable pieces: the contract's address and its Application Binary Interface, or ABI. The address is the unique location on the blockchain where the contract lives. Think of it like a postal address for a house; without it your requests cannot find the contract. The ABI is a JSON description of the contract's functions, their inputs and outputs, and events. It tells your library how to encode function arguments into the low-level call format and how to decode returned data. Concretely, when you compile Solidity using a tool like Hardhat or Remix, the compiler outputs the ABI. In Web3. js you typically create an instance with new web3. eth. Contract(ABI, address). In Ethers. js you call new ethers. Contract(address, ABI, provider). If the ABI doesn't match the deployed contract, the library cannot find function signatures and calls will fail with function not found or invalid arguments. A practical tip: always update the frontend ABI when contract interfaces change. Example: if SimpleData exposes message and counter, your ABI must include those getter signatures so your script can call them. Misconception check: the ABI is not executable code; it's only a description used to encode calls. The core takeaway is that address locates and ABI describes — both are required for reliable reads.

keyIdea.title: Instance rule
keyIdea.text: Address locates the contract; ABI describes its interface. Both are required to instantiate a usable contract object.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Contract Instance
Definition

A contract instance binds an ABI to a specific address so your library can encode requests and decode responses against a deployed contract.

  • Address: unique identifier on-chain.
  • ABI: JSON blueprint of functions, inputs, outputs.
  • Instance: the runtime object you call methods on.
Analogy
Address is the house number; ABI is the house blueprint telling you where each room is and what it contains.
Key Takeaway

Always pair the current deployed address with the matching ABI to avoid function lookup errors.

Instantiation examples
// Web3.js
const myContract = new web3.eth.Contract(CONTRACT_ABI, CONTRACT_ADDRESS);

// Ethers.js
const myContract = new ethers.Contract(CONTRACT_ADDRESS, CONTRACT_ABI, provider);
Common mistake
Using an ABI from a different contract version leads to "function not found" errors.
Pro tip
Store ABI alongside the deployed address in your deployment artifacts so the frontend can pick the correct pair automatically.

screens.title: Reading with Web3.js: contract.methods.call()
screens.subtitle: Create the contract and use .call() to fetch view/pure data

narration.text: Web3. js exposes contract functions through the methods property on a contract instance. Once you have new web3. eth. Contract(ABI, address), call read-only functions using the call method on the desired method: await myContract. methods. someGetter(). call(). This executes the function locally on the connected node and returns the decoded result. In practice you will often read public state variables first; the compiler generates a getter that appears in the ABI, so you can call myContract. methods. message(). call() to retrieve the string. A concrete example from SimpleData: call multiplyByTwo with an argument ten and log the result; the call returns immediately and will not create a transaction. Always wrap calls in try catch to handle network errors or reverts. An important misstep to avoid is using. call() on functions that you expect to modify state. Even if. call() returns a value, it never persists state changes — that requires sending a transaction with a signer. Also be mindful of numeric types: web3 returns big numbers as strings or BN objects depending on configuration, so convert them before display. Finally, test your calls against a local node like Ganache to confirm ABI and address correctness, since remote nodes or mismatched ABIs produce common function-not-found errors.

keyIdea.title: Web3.js read pattern
keyIdea.text: Use contract.methods.fnName(...).call() for view/pure functions; always wrap in try/catch and convert numeric returns appropriately.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Web3.js Read
Code walkthrough
// Assuming web3 is initialized
const myContract = new web3.eth.Contract(CONTRACT_ABI, CONTRACT_ADDRESS);

async function readDataWeb3(){
  try{
    const message = await myContract.methods.message().call();
    const counter = await myContract.methods.counter().call();
    const doubled = await myContract.methods.multiplyByTwo(10).call();
    console.log(message, counter.toString(), doubled.toString());
  } catch (err){
    console.error('Web3.js Read Error:', err.message);
  }
}
Example
Calling multiplyByTwo(10) returns 20 immediately from the node.
Common mistake
Expecting call() to mutate state. It only reads.
Why it matters
Using .call() keeps your DApp responsive and avoids gas costs while showing current on-chain values.
Key Takeaway

Web3.js exposes methods via .methods and .call() runs a local node execution. Convert numeric returns for UI use.

Check your understanding
If you see function not found, confirm the ABI contains the function signature and the address points to the expected contract.

screens.title: Reading with Ethers.js: provider-only Contract
screens.subtitle: Instantiate with a provider; call functions as regular async methods

narration.text: Ethers. js simplifies read-only interactions by letting you treat contract methods as normal async functions when the contract is connected to a provider. You create a contract instance with new ethers. Contract(address, ABI, provider). No signer is required for view and pure functions. After instantiation, just await myContract. someGetter() and ethers will execute a call behind the scenes and return decoded values. For example, with SimpleData you can await myContract. message() to get the message string, await myContract. counter() to get the numeric counter, and await myContract. multiplyByTwo(10) to compute a pure function result. Error handling still matters: wrap calls in try catch to capture connectivity issues, revert messages, or ABI mismatches. A key difference from Web3. js is the more direct method invocation style and the fact that BigNumber results are returned as ethers BigNumber objects — remember to convert them to string using toString() before rendering. Also understand that Ethers will automatically route view/pure calls through the provider; if you attach a signer later, the same contract object can be used for transactions, but read-only use should remain provider-only to avoid accidental transaction signing. Misconception check: calling a method on a contract instance does not imply a transaction if the instance is connected only to a provider.

keyIdea.title: Ethers read pattern
keyIdea.text: Instantiate with address, ABI, and provider. Call methods directly and convert BigNumber results as needed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Ethers.js Read
Ethers.js example
const provider = new ethers.providers.JsonRpcProvider(GANACHE_RPC_URL);
const myContract = new ethers.Contract(CONTRACT_ADDRESS, CONTRACT_ABI, provider);

async function readDataEthers(){
  try{
    const message = await myContract.message();
    const counter = await myContract.counter();
    const doubled = await myContract.multiplyByTwo(10);
    console.log(message, counter.toString(), doubled.toString());
  } catch(err){
    console.error('Ethers.js Read Error:', err.message);
  }
}
Example
Awaiting myContract.getMessageLength() returns a number from the node via provider.
Pro tip
Call toString() on BigNumber returns to presentable strings for UIs.
Misconception
Using a signer with the same contract object will permit transactions; ensure provider-only when you only want reads.
Key Takeaway

Ethers reads look like normal async calls; they are executed locally via the provider and require conversion of BigNumber values for display.

Check
If a call errors, compare the ABI and address to the deployed contract and verify the provider URL is correct.

screens.title: Public State Variables and Auto-Generated Getters
screens.subtitle: How Solidity exposes public variables to external callers

narration.text: Solidity automatically generates a getter function for any state variable declared public. This means that if your contract declares string public message or uint public counter, the compiler will add a function with the same name that returns the variable's value. From the frontend you can call these getters exactly like any view function — for Web3. js call myContract. methods. message(). call(); for Ethers. js await myContract. message(). The convenience reduces boilerplate and simplifies data access: you don't need to write explicit getter functions in Solidity to expose simple state. A concrete example is the SimpleData contract where message returns a string and counter returns an unsigned integer; the getters are included in the ABI and will be present in the compiled output. Be mindful that complex types like arrays or mappings require indexed accessors or helper functions because the compiler cannot export entire dynamic mappings as a single getter. A common misconception is believing public means accessible for mutation by external callers; public only controls visibility and provides a read accessor — it does not allow arbitrary modification. Key practical point: rely on these auto-generated getters for straightforward reads, but write specific read functions when you need aggregated or computed views of state.

keyIdea.title: Public getter rule
keyIdea.text: Declaring a state variable public creates a compiled getter function, simplifying frontend reads without extra Solidity code.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Public Variables
How it works

When a variable is declared public, the compiler generates a view function with the same name that returns its value. That function appears in the ABI and can be invoked from the frontend.

Example: message and counter in SimpleData are accessible through message() and counter() getters.
Limitations: mappings and nested arrays need specific accessors for efficient reads.
Misconception: public does not mean writable by external callers; it only provides visibility and a getter.
Concrete example
Call myContract.methods.message().call() in Web3.js or await myContract.message() in Ethers.js to retrieve the message string stored in the contract.
Why it matters

Auto-generated getters reduce Solidity code and make common frontend reads straightforward and reliable.

Check your understanding
If you need aggregated data, write a view function that computes the result rather than relying on several auto-getters in the frontend.

screens.title: view vs pure functions
screens.subtitle: Understand the difference and when to use each

narration.text: In Solidity, view and pure functions are both read-only from the blockchain's perspective, but they have different constraints and use cases. A view function declares it will not modify state; it may read state variables but does not change storage. Use view for queries that depend on contract data, like returning a counter value or computing derived information from stored values. A pure function promises not to read or modify contract state. It only operates on its input parameters and returns a result derived solely from those inputs. Pure is ideal for utility calculations such as multiplyByTwo in our SimpleData example. Both view and pure calls are free when invoked off-chain through a provider because they do not create transactions. However, you should choose the correct modifier when designing your contract to make the intent clear and to allow frontend callers to safely call the function without expecting side effects. A common mistake is marking a function view when it accidentally alters state through a library or an external call; the compiler will usually enforce this, but careful review is essential. Example: getMessageLength should be view because it reads message length from storage, while multiplyByTwo is pure because it operates only on the provided number. The takeaway: use view for state-dependent reads and pure for self-contained calculations.

keyIdea.title: Read-only types
keyIdea.text: view reads state without modifying it; pure neither reads nor writes state. Choose appropriately to express intent and enable safe frontend calls.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › view vs pure
view

Reads contract state but does not change storage. Use for getters and queries dependent on stored values.

Example: function getMessageLength() public view returns (uint) { return bytes(message).length; }
When to use: Any function that reads variables to compute answers for the UI.
pure

Does not read or write contract state. It performs computations solely on inputs and returns results.

Example: function multiplyByTwo(uint _num) public pure returns (uint) { return _num * 2; }
When to use: Utility functions and deterministic calculations independent of storage.
Key Takeaway

Both are gas-free for frontend reads via provider, but their contract-level guarantees differ: view may read state; pure cannot touch state at all.

screens.title: call() vs send(): When to read and when to transact
screens.subtitle: Understand the behavioral and cost differences between read and write operations

narration.text: Distinguishing between call and send is essential to avoid costly mistakes in a DApp. call executes a function locally on a node and returns its result without creating a transaction, requiring no gas and no signer. send, by contrast, submits a signed transaction which is mined and changes on-chain state; it requires a signer, gas, and user confirmation. For read-only functions declared view or pure, always use call or the provider-style invocation in Ethers. js. If you attempt to use call on a state-modifying function, you may observe the code path execute locally and a return value appear in your console, but any state changes will not persist — this leads to confusing bugs where the UI appears to work but the blockchain state is unchanged. Conversely, calling send on a pure or view function is unnecessary and will either fail or waste gas if forced. A practical example: to increment a counter you must send a transaction from a signer account; to display the current counter value you call the getter. Also account for asynchronous latency: send returns transaction receipts after mining, while call returns results almost immediately from the node. Misconception to avoid: call cannot simulate gas costs or revert side effects accurately for transactions; use it purely for reading. The rule: read with call, write with send.

keyIdea.title: Read vs write
keyIdea.text: call is for local, gas-free reads; send is for signed state changes that cost gas. Use each for its intended purpose.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › call() vs send()
call()

Executes locally on the node, returns decoded result, no gas, no signer required. Ideal for view/pure functions and public getters.

Behavior: Immediate result, no state change.
Use when: Displaying state in UI, computing derived values that don't alter storage.
send()

Sends a signed transaction to change state, requires a signer and gas, and returns a transaction receipt after mining.

Behavior: Alters storage and costs gas.
Use when: Performing state updates like transfer, increment, or any write operation.
Key Takeaway

Read with call, write with send. Never substitute call for a write and expect persistence; test writes against a signer on a local node.

screens.title: Common mistakes: ABI, address, and function-not-found
screens.subtitle: Diagnose and fix the top frontend read errors

narration.text: Many read-time failures come from three recurring issues: an incorrect contract address, an outdated ABI, or calling the wrong function signature. If your frontend logs function not found or invalid arguments, first verify the deployed address is the one your frontend uses. Addresses change with each deployment, especially on local testnets. Second, ensure the ABI in your frontend matches the contract's current compiled ABI. If you changed function names or parameters and didn't update the ABI, the signature will not match and calls will fail. Third, confirm you are calling the generated getter for public variables or the exact view/pure function name. Typo mistakes are surprisingly common. For diagnostics, run a simple read script against Ganache that calls a known getter and prints the result — if it works there, the issue is likely a provider or network mismatch in your app. When you see a revert in a call, examine the contract code for require statements that may stop execution or use console error messages in local tests to capture revert reasons. Always wrap calls in try catch to capture and log the raw error message, then map it to a friendly user-facing message. For example, show "Unable to fetch contract data — check network" instead of raw stack traces. The pragmatic approach is to validate address and ABI first, then provider connectivity, then function signatures.

keyIdea.title: Diagnostic order
keyIdea.text: When a read fails: verify address, then ABI, then provider connectivity and function signature to find the root cause quickly.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Common mistakes
Top failure modes
  1. Wrong address: Deployments change addresses; confirm the frontend has the current one.
  2. Outdated ABI: If the contract interface changed, update the ABI or calls will not match signatures.
  3. Provider mismatch: Pointing to the wrong network or node can cause unreachable calls.
Diagnostic script: Run the readContract.js script against Ganache to isolate ABI/address issues before debugging the UI.
Example error mapping
Raw: function not found — likely ABI mismatch.
User message: "Unable to load contract data — update ABI or redeploy."

screens.title: Error handling for read-only interactions
screens.subtitle: Wrap calls, map errors, and show user-friendly feedback

narration.text: Robust error handling separates a good DApp from a fragile one. Always wrap asynchronous reads in try catch blocks and inspect the error to decide user-facing messaging. Network errors, ABI mismatches, and revert traces are common categories. For network or provider failures, inform the user to check their connection or the node status. For ABI mismatches, suggest a developer action like updating the ABI or redeploying the contract. For reverts, capture the revert reason where available on a local node, and display a concise message. In code, log the full error to the console for debugging, but present a friendly summary in the UI. Example pattern: try the call; on failure, if error message contains "function not found" say "contract interface mismatch"; if it contains "replacement transaction underpriced" or similar, guide the user to check network settings. For Ethers. js BigNumber handling, also guard conversions inside the try block because toString can throw if unexpected. Finally, implement retries for transient network glitches with exponential backoff and a clear progress indicator. Misconception: do not expose raw error traces or node stack traces to end users — they are confusing and may leak sensitive runtime details.

keyIdea.title: Error handling rule
keyIdea.text: Wrap reads in try/catch, log details for debugging, and present concise, actionable messages to the user.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Error Handling
Pattern
try{
  const result = await myContract.someGetter();
  // convert and display
} catch(err){
  console.error(err);
  // map to friendly message and show to user
}
Retry strategy
For transient network errors, retry with exponential backoff and a progress indicator.
Don't do this
Expose raw stack traces to end users. Map them instead to helpful instructions.
Key Takeaway

Graceful error handling improves user trust: log details, show short actions, and avoid technical overload.

Example mapping
Map "function not found" to "Contract interface mismatch" and suggest updating the ABI or redeploying.

screens.title: Deploy and read: SimpleData walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Deploy to Ganache, copy ABI & address, run readContract.js with Web3 and Ethers

narration.text: This guided walkthrough outlines the steps to deploy SimpleData to a local Ganache instance and verify read-only interactions. First, compile the SimpleData contract in your tool of choice and deploy it to Ganache, noting the deployed contract address printed by the tool. Next, copy the compiled ABI JSON and the address into readContract. js placeholders. For Web3. js, create a new Web3 provider pointed at Ganache and instantiate new web3. eth. Contract(ABI, ADDRESS). For Ethers. js, create a JsonRpcProvider with the same Ganache URL and instantiate new ethers. Contract(ADDRESS, ABI, provider). Run the script node readContract. js and observe console output for message, counter, getMessageLength, and multiplyByTwo. If you get an error, check the GANACHE_RPC_URL, ensure Ganache is running, and confirm ABI entries include the called functions. Also remember to call toString() on numeric results for clear terminal display. This activity is designed to cement the full flow: compile → deploy → copy ABI/address → instantiate in frontend → call and handle results. Misconception check: do not expect calls to update on-chain state; only send transactions if you want persistence. The hands-on loop is the fastest way to internalize instantiation, calling, and troubleshooting patterns for read-only operations.

keyIdea.title: Activity outcome
keyIdea.text: Deploy SimpleData, run readContract.js with ABI and address, and verify outputs to confirm your read-only integration works.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Hands-on Activity
Step-by-step
  1. Compile SimpleData and deploy to Ganache; copy the deployed address.
  2. Copy the compiled ABI JSON into readContract.js CONTRACT_ABI placeholder.
  3. Set GANACHE_RPC_URL and CONTRACT_ADDRESS in the script.
  4. Run node readContract.js and inspect outputs for message and counter.
Terminal expectations
--- Reading with Web3.js ---
Web3.js Message: Hello Cohortia!
Web3.js Counter: 42
Web3.js Doubled (10): 20

--- Reading with Ethers.js ---
Ethers.js Message: Hello Cohortia!
Ethers.js Counter: 42
Ethers.js Doubled (10): 20
Key Takeaway

Running the script end-to-end validates ABI, address, and provider settings, and helps you spot mismatches quickly.

screens.title: Handling numeric types and BigNumber conversion
screens.subtitle: Convert BigNumber results for display and calculations

narration.text: Numeric values from contracts often arrive as BigNumber objects rather than native JavaScript numbers. Both Web3. js and Ethers. js represent large unsigned integers in a form that preserves precision beyond JavaScript's safe integer range. When reading values like counters or token balances, convert BigNumber to string using toString() for terminal logging or UI text. If you need numeric math in JavaScript, use a BigNumber library or convert to Number only when you are sure the value is within the safe range. Example: after await myContract. counter(), call counter. toString() before placing it in the DOM to avoid truncated or incorrect values. A common oversight is using arithmetic operators directly on BigNumber objects; these will not behave as expected. Instead, use library methods for addition or multiplication and then convert to string. When dealing with Ethers. js, the returned object exposes toString() and other helpers to format decimals. Also be mindful of token decimals: you may need to divide by 10 to the power of decimals for human-readable values. For SimpleData, counter is small and safe to convert, but in production token balances and supply figures must be handled with precise conversion to avoid display bugs. The practical rule: always inspect the returned type and use toString() for safe, readable output.

keyIdea.title: Numeric handling
keyIdea.text: Convert BigNumber results to strings with toString() and use safe libraries for numerical math to preserve precision.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › BigNumber Handling
Convert before display
// Ethers.js result
const counter = await myContract.counter();
console.log(counter.toString());

// Avoid: console.log(counter + 1) on a BigNumber
Tip: Use libraries like BN or BigNumber when you need arithmetic. For UI, use toString() to render values safely.
Decimal tokens: Remember to divide by 10**decimals to present human-readable balances.
Key Takeaway

Always inspect returned types. Convert BigNumber to string for display; use safe math libraries for calculations.

Common mistake
Performing native JS arithmetic on BigNumber leads to incorrect results or errors.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from read-only interactions

narration.text: Here are the concise concepts to keep in mind. First, a contract instance requires the address and ABI so your library can encode calls and decode results. Second, view and pure functions are read-only: use provider-only calls to fetch their results without gas. Third, public state variables auto-generate getters you can call directly from the frontend. These three ideas form the foundation of safe, efficient read-only DApp behavior. When you combine them with careful error handling and correct numeric conversions, your UI will reflect on-chain state reliably and with minimal cost. Key Concepts means address + abi + provider = reliable read-only contract interactions; handle errors and convert numeric types for safe display.. In practical terms, what to remember from read-only interactions. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Memory hook
keyIdea.text: Address + ABI + Provider = reliable read-only contract interactions; handle errors and convert numeric types for safe display.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Key Concepts
Contract Address
Unique on-chain location used to address deployed contracts.
ABI
JSON blueprint describing functions, inputs, outputs, and events for encoding and decoding calls.
view / pure
Read-only functions: view can read state, pure cannot read state. Both are gas-free when called off-chain.
Summary takeaway
Use the correct ABI/address pair, call view and pure functions through a provider, convert numeric returns, and handle errors gracefully to build dependable read-only DApp features.
